newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Doctors upbeat on Yeltsin but wait for op goes on.
newsitem.headline: Doctors upbeat on Yeltsin but wait for op goes on.

text.p: Doctors have declared Russian President Boris Yeltsin fit enough to undergo heart surgery but said the operation must be put off for at least six weeks.

The decision by a team of cardiologists on Wednesday calmed fears that the 65-year-old president's overall condition was too bad for him to survive surgery, but condemned Russia to weeks more of political uncertainty.

"After reviewing all facts I am very encouraged to tell you that the operation is needed, that it should provide excellent results," said U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, who was present at the discussion on Yeltsin's condition.
"There is no reason why the president should not be restored to full normal activity," he told reporters after the doctors saw Yeltsin at Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital.
Yeltsin disappeared from public view just before he was re-elected last July.

One of the president's doctors said at the weekend that Yeltsin had suffered a third heart attack in late June or early July. Speculation had been mounting that the Kremlin leader might have other unannounced problems which ruled out surgery.
The same doctor, cardiologist Renat Akchurin, said on Thursday that the operation would go ahead but a delay would increase Yeltsin's chances of coming through it.
"If we operate now, I would say the chance (of success) is about 80 percent, but we hope that in six weeks the percentage would be close to 100," he said.
The doctors' comments must have come as some relief to Kremlin aides hoping to keep Yeltsin in power for as long as possible.

But Yeltsin will be out of the Kremlin waiting for surgery for at least six more weeks and DeBakey said patients usually needed at least another six weeks to recover from the bypass operation he needs -- grafting in veins from the leg to relieve clogged heart arteries.
That leaves plenty of scope for more of the jostling for position in the Kremlin which political analysts say has intensified since Yeltsin fell ill.
"There will be a lot of uncertainty for a long time and decisions will be put off. What we face is unpredictability and stagnation," said one political analyst, Lilia Shevtsova.
The main power rivals are widely thought to be Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and security tsar Alexander Lebed.

The stolid Chernomyrdin has kept a relatively low profile but Lebed has made a series of controversial statements in the last few days which have highlighted his tendency to make comments out of step with others in Russia's leadership.

In the latest such incident, Lebed raised eyebrows in Washington with comments to the newspaper Vechernyaya Moskva in which he condemned U.S. missile attacks on Iraq earlier this month and said that if that happened to Russia: "I would hit back instantly. With everything we've got."
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the remarks were "quite puzzling to us. We feel our relationship with Russia is on a very good footing."
